chapter_theme: Paripadal 12, to the Vaiyai: the flood coming down from the hills with their trees, the town of Madurai dressing and riding out to meet it, the music at the ford, the onlookers' gossip of a husband's straying look, his wife's garland-blows and coloured water and the flood that ends her sulk, the river muddy, clear and blood-red as the war-king's river, and the festival whose fame the world cannot hold.

comparisons.tenor: the Vaiyai's coming down in flood

paripadal:12:1-8.reading: Clouds lit by wind-struck lightning spread darkness over the sky and close round the soft hills without pause, the rain-washed slopes shed their flowers, and the Vaiyai comes down carrying the bright-hooded cobra, eaglewood, vazhai, gnemai, sandal and the fragrant thagaram, gnaazhal and deodar, its sweet water and wind seeming to make for the full sea.
paripadal:12:1-8.nuance: The song opens not at Madurai but at the source: the river's load is a list of hill things (kurinji trees and a hill snake), so the flood that reaches the town in line 9 arrives as the hills' gift. The simile of line 7 gives the river a will (முன்னியது, 'aimed at'): it seems bound for the sea, though the town will claim it first.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of the river, sung as praise of the Vaiyai: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the watchers' longing, risen above the flood

paripadal:12:9-35.reading: Hearing that the cool lovely Vaiyai has come strewing flowers and beating against Madurai's wall, the town makes ready: some put on gleaming jewels, some set gold-leaf flower ornaments, some change their eaglewood paste for smoked sandal, some dress their dark hair or bind in flowers, some put on fitting cloth and clasped bead strings, some bathe in scented oil, polish their mirrors and study their colour and glow, and chew fragrant betel; men and women in bangles, armlets, anklets and honeyed garlands, fragrant from a league off, ride gentle horses, sit on she-elephants like a host of swans, spur swift horses and tuskers and belled chariots, crowding in ever greater haste with dancing everywhere, so that the water came to be Koodal's talk and the crowd came to fill its banks; the flood rose over the banks, and the watchers' longing rose as if it had seized the flood.
paripadal:12:9-35.nuance: Lines 11 to 22 are a catalogue built on the repeated -ஓரும் ('some ... some'), the whole town as a list of acts of dressing; the river's arrival is first a rumour (எனக் கேட்டு, line 10) and the festival is the town's answer to news. Lines 32 to 35 balance the water and the crowd in matched clauses (வந்தன்று ... வந்தன்று), and the last simile turns it round: not the flood taking the people, but their longing taking the flood.

thinai_evidence.note: the town going out to the flood, praise of the river's festival: paadaan

paripadal:12:36-44.reading: At the front ford the voices of those standing in their finery rise together, not one but many, and no one can hear them all; of what can be heard, the flute sounds in tune, the muzhavu roars with the maththari, thadaari, thannumai and maguli drums, all measured together on the beat, none falling behind, and the young women with their bright even-wristed forearms keep the time: look at them.
paripadal:12:36-44.nuance: The poet stages the limits of report: the crowd's words cannot all be heard (lines 37 to 39), so he picks out some (கேள்வி கேட்டன சிலசில), and the episodes that follow are offered as samples overheard at the ford. The rhythm of the drums is kept by women's hands, the festival's order made visible in the same crowd that is speaking at once.

thinai_evidence.note: the music and noise of the festival crowd at the ford: paadaan

paripadal:12:45-74.reading: Voices in the crowd: one says, is she not ashamed, friend, the woman who said he had enjoyed the beauty of a graceless courtesan's shoulders and left her, and now rides the she-elephant in the flood with that man; another, that the man who eyes the breasts of a slender girl in the company is a leaky-minded weakling; another, that a woman who heeds neither the scratches nor the words, whose colour has changed and who has followed the man down the road, shows that restraint takes fright and leaves once love has come; another bids them look at the 'pure' one who, having eyed a woman's necklace and breasts while a goddess-like woman with a nectar look watched, is beaten by his wife with her garland, his hands tied tight with her ornament, and, seeing no fault in himself, bows and asks to be told it; when she says a woman looked at him, he pleads that he never knew the woman was one of false oaths, and to his true oaths she says 'false' and twists his words; sulking and refusing him, she flings a ball of flower-coloured water, and as if from the wound of her spear-like eyes his blood runs, his heart fails and he sinks to the ground; then, troubled and afraid of a scar on his strong chest, all her quarrel passes, and the Vaiyai's flood, as always, brings her back to her lover's lovely breast.
paripadal:12:45-74.nuance: Every episode is reported speech of onlookers (என்மரும், 'some say'), so the oodal is seen from outside, as gossip and spectacle, not voiced by the lovers. தூயவனைக் காண்மின் (line 60) is irony: the onlooker has just said the man eyed another woman's breasts. The coloured water of the festival game becomes, by metaphor, the blood of the wound her glance made, and the reconciliation is credited at the end not to either lover but to the river (வல்லதால், வையைப் புனல்): the sulk scene is told as praise of the Vaiyai. Who swears and who answers in lines 61 to 64 is hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan, the husband's straying look and the wife's sulk at the river bathing: marutham

comparisons.tenor: the wife's garland, used as a stick
the coloured water running down the husband

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: onlookers at the ford speak to one another (நாணாள்கொல்தோழி; காண்மின்); the colophon gives no thurai

paripadal:12:75-85.reading: So it goes; with jasmine, mauval, fragrant champak, alli, kazhuneer, lotus, aambal, kullai, vakulam, kurukkaththi, paathiri, the clustered naagam, naravam and surapunnai all smelling sweet, the two banks run muddy; then, settling and clearing, the river from the great dark hill, held by dams spread over the rock beds, shows heaven's beauty in the reflection of its water; and in the morning of the rains it is red with turbid blood, the river of the king whose army kills in war.
paripadal:12:75-85.nuance: Three states of the one river follow each other: muddy with flowers, clear enough to mirror heaven, and red as blood in the monsoon. The last is turned to the king's praise: the flood's red silt is read as the blood of his wars, so the river is named by its owner's killing (போர் அடு தானையான் யாறு). The flower list mixes plants of every landscape (jasmine of mullai, lotus and aambal of the fields, punnai of the shore), the river gathering them all.

thinai_evidence.note: the river praised in its beauty and as the war-king's river: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the red asoka flower hanging at her ear
the woman swaying as she walks

paripadal:12:86-91.reading: Having set in her ear a fragrant asoka flower that hangs red like an ear-ring of fire-worked gold, swaying like a flowering creeper, stepping foot after foot, the good woman with even-wristed forearms straightened her garland on the breast of the bangled lovely one: look, she is with her own.
paripadal:12:86-91.nuance: A single festival figure singled out for the audience (காண்மின், 'look'). Whose breast (ஆகம்) the garland is set on, and whether கேள் in line 91 is her lover or her companion, cannot be fixed from these lines; if it is her lover, this is a small scene of union after the quarrel of lines 45 to 74.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman of the festival crowd described for praise: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the gem-clear water full of floating flowers

paripadal:12:92-101.reading: The gem-clear water is full like a cloth sewn with flowers; 'the flood!' says the old town, its talk swelling, and the beauty rises above the talk; the crowd clashes and jostles again and again; the thagaram and sandal washed from chests turn the sand to mire; with the water that soaks the clothes the banks take on darkness; the sky lets loose, and so is the festival flood: old town of pleasure, beauty and clamour, many good things, many good things, Vaiyai, this flower-topped world cannot hold your fame.
paripadal:12:92-101.nuance: The close is a run of short clauses each ending in -அன்று, as if listing the day's events at speed, and it ends on a hyperbole of measure: the world, though crowned with flowers, is too small for the river's fame. Several clauses (போர் ஏற்றன்று, நவின்று; கரை கார் ஏற்றன்று; விசும்பு கடி விட்டன்று) are terse and their sense is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: closing praise of the river and its festival: paadaan

links.note: Kalittokai 67.3-5 says the Vaiyai beating against the wall (மதில் பொரூஉம்) is the only enemy the walled town has known; Paripadal 12.9 has the town hear that the Vaiyai has come beating against Madurai's wall (மதுரை மதில் பொரூஉம்) and rush out in finery to meet it.
links.teaches: The akam poem turns the river's assault on the wall into a boast that no army ever reached Madurai, and the hymn shows what that only siege was like inside the walls, a summons that sends the whole town to dress and ride out, so together they show the flood as the city's one welcomed attack, the festival standing where war stands for other towns.

links.note: In Kalittokai 67.6-9 the wife says she will sulk when her husband comes showing the wounds and scars (புண், வடு) that other women's garlands (கோதையால் அலைத்த) left on him, and her heart gives way when she sees him; in Paripadal 12.57-73 the wife herself beats her husband with her garland (கமழ் கோதை கோலாப் புடைத்து), then fears a scar on his chest (வடு அஞ்சி) and her quarrel passes.
links.teaches: In the Kalittokai the garland-wound is evidence against the husband, written on him by rival women, while in the hymn the wife wields the garland herself and her fear of the scar is what ends her sulk, so the pair shows the garland-blow as a festival game of the Vaiyai town whose meaning, accusation or claim, depends on whose hand struck it.

links.note: Kural 1321 has the woman say that though he has no fault, his grace has the power to bring on a sulk; in Paripadal 12.55-60 the man has eyed another woman's breasts, and when beaten he 'sees no fault' (பிழை ஒன்றும் காணான்) and bows asking to be told it, and the onlookers call him the pure one (தூயவனைக் காண்மின்).
links.teaches: The couplet takes the faultless lover of the oodal at the woman's word, while the hymn shows a crowd that has watched him look and mocks his innocence as he begs to hear his fault, so together they show that the faultless husband of the sulk was a convention its audience knew to be a pose, and that the Kural's version is the inside view of a scene the festival saw from outside.

links.note: Paripadal 7.65-76 has a woman, angry that her lover looked at the bathers, punish him in the river; Paripadal 12.55-74 has the same offence of looking at another woman at the flood and the same sulk, carried through the blow and his fall to her return to his breast, which the poet credits to the Vaiyai's flood (வல்லதால், வையைப் புனல்).
links.teaches: Song 7 leaves the river quarrel at the lover's punishment, while song 12 carries the same quarrel to its making-up and gives the river the credit, so the two Vaiyai songs show that the oodal episode was told in the hymns in order to praise the flood as the reconciler, the go-between that akam poems give to a friend or a bard.

links.note: Kalavazhi Narpathu 30 likens the pooled blood of the battlefield, dragging killed elephants, to a flood that rolls boulders down the hill (மலையுருட்டு நீர்போல்); Paripadal 12.84-85 sees the Vaiyai in the morning of the rains red with turbid blood (கலிழ் செங் குருதித்தே) and names it the river of the king whose army kills in war.
links.teaches: The war poem uses the hill torrent as the image for battle blood and the hymn uses battle blood as the image for the monsoon torrent, so held together they show the comparison running both ways for Tamil poets: the king's killing is a flood and his river's flood is his killing, the river's redness counting as his fame.

links.note: Kural 1064 says the dignity that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for all the world to hold (இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளா); Paripadal 12.101 ends by telling the Vaiyai that this flower-topped world cannot hold its fame (நின் புகழ் கொள்ளாது, இம் மலர் தலை உலகே).
links.teaches: The same measure, a greatness the world is too small to hold, is given by the hymn to a river's yearly plenty and by the Kural to a destitute man's refusal to ask, so the pair shows the ethical book taking the praise formula of abundance and fixing it on the one thing that has no abundance at all.

source_issues: Paripadal 12: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; only the subject வையை, the poet நல்வழுதியார், the music நன்னாகனார் and the pan பாலையாழ் (a musical mode, not a thinai) are given.

Paripadal 12 lines 9, 29, 38 and 39 are flagged as lines once taken for modern headings; read by eye they are verse: line 9 opens the reported news, line 29 continues the list of riders, and lines 38-39 complete the sentence begun at the end of line 37 (அவை / எல்லாம் ... அவை / கில்லா). They are kept.

Paripadal 12 has 101 lines but the source numbers its last line 100, and its printed number 60 stands on line 59; our line numbers follow show, not the printed ones. The short line 75 (என ஆங்கு) may be the one the source did not count.
Paripadal 12 line 6: ஞாழ்லும் reads as a misprint for ஞாழலும்.
Paripadal 12 line 11: வேயு மோரும் is one word split, read வேயுமோரும் as in line 16.
Paripadal 12 line 2 கிளையொடு and line 23 வளையொடு have the vowel sign ொ restored (flags); line 2 is not confirmed by sangamtamil.com.
Paripadal 12 lines 61-64 (who swears the oaths and who calls them false) and lines 94-98 (a run of terse clauses) are hard to construe; lines 89-91 do not fix whose breast the garland is set on.
